overview: This file combines a Department of State cross-reference sheet and a 1938 consular despatch concerning medical relief for sick and disabled foreign seamen in Japan, together with an apparently unrelated 1930 Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum assessing a report on the Japanese press. The central maritime document records Yokohama officials’ statement that Japan had no government hospitals providing medical services to seamen from foreign vessels. The additional memorandum praises a broad study of the Japanese press and approves its restricted circulation to responsible correspondents.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch 1138 from Yokohama
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects readers to a medical-relief file containing Johansen’s October 15, 1938 despatch on the treatment of sick and disabled seamen by foreign governments.
subfiles.summary: This filing note identifies Despatch 1138 from Yokohama, dated October 15, 1938, and attributes it to Johansen. It directs the reader to file 136.7 Medical Relief/30 for information concerning the treatment of sick and disabled seamen by foreign governments; the OCR’s “women” is evidently a misreading of “seamen.”

subfiles.title: Despatch 1138 on medical services for foreign seamen in Japan
subfiles.from: Berge R. Johansen, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Johansen reports the result of an inquiry into Japanese government medical provision for sick and disabled seamen from foreign vessels.
subfiles.summary: Responding to the Department’s mimeographed instruction of September 3, 1938, Vice Consul Johansen consulted local government officials in Yokohama. They advised that Japan had no government hospitals supplying medical services to sick and disabled seamen of foreign vessels. The page is identified as a true copy of the signed original.

subfiles.title: Division memorandum assessing a report on “The Japanese Press”
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs (initialed RSM)
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum evaluates a comprehensive report on the history, organization, ethics, and influence of the Japanese press.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum calls the report an excellent, balanced, and useful treatment of the Japanese press, covering its historical background, circulation, composition, management, ethics, and influence. It notes that some conclusions about press influence may be overly optimistic. The writer sees no objection to showing the report to Mr. Hulen or another responsible correspondent, provided that quotation or reference is restricted.

interest: The 1938 despatch offers concise evidence about the limits of state-supported maritime medical welfare in prewar Japan and about the State Department’s comparative inquiry into foreign treatment of seamen. Its accompanying cross-reference illustrates the Department’s decimal filing and redistribution practices. The seemingly unrelated 1930 press memorandum is valuable both for its assessment of Japanese media and for what it reveals about controlled State Department sharing of internal reports with journalists; its presence also documents the heterogeneous or imperfect composition of archival subject files.
